rv.q: This is a quieter wow of a show.
Washburn and Cosson’s latest collaboration is a powerful exploration of why we continue to make up stories and act them out for others, even if we know they cannot say what we truly feel.
Beautiful and fascinating, it is by no means satisfying.

Then in the final 10 minutes or so of the drama, Washburn suddenly rockets the story off – by way of a trial-by-fire pageant the kids have enacted – into a brief, blazing world of allegory and symbolism the meaning of which baffled me completely.

Aside from the fact that you may not always be able to follow the play which has its own reasons for being obscure, you will have trouble being able to put your finger on the message but leave the theater wondering what did it all mean.
Unlike Mr. Burns , though, the elements don't quite cohere, and the play fails to reward the mental effort required to piece its ideas together.

Here, the opacity just feels like Washburn and Cosson have decided the world of the play is less interesting than its formal qualities–and the result is a cornucopia of experiments across genre and style that add up to an inert whole, albeit performed by an excellent ensemble of off-Broadway stalwarts.
To see The Burning Cauldron of Fiery Fire is to be lost in a world of private meaning; in the script, Washburn writes, "Not a moment of this should be played for satire."
Washburn’s latest play is uneven in conveying what her message is about with this commune.
But far too much of The Burning Cauldron feels like an inchoate project that hasn’t had enough time to settle in and take shape.

cn.t: Washburn's enigmatic commune drama divides critics, with most finding it frustratingly opaque and emotionally distant. Praise goes to its ambitious exploration of grief and storytelling, but many criticize characters who feel more like seminar students than humans.
